analysis.one_liner: Applies ACA protections, including preexisting-condition coverage, to short-term health plans.
analysis.headline: The bill never got a committee hearing or a vote; it was introduced in July 2018 and referred to the House Energy and Commerce Committee, which took no action before Congress ended in January 2019.
analysis.plain_summary: Short-term, limited-duration health plans are cheaper than ACA-compliant plans because they are exempt from the Affordable Care Act's rules: they can refuse people, charge more, or exclude coverage for preexisting conditions, and can leave patients with large uncovered bills. This bill would fold short-term plans into the legal definition of individual health insurance, so they would have to follow the same rules as regular plans, including covering preexisting conditions. It was referred to committee and never went any further.
analysis.who_benefits: People who buy or consider buying short-term health plans, especially anyone with a preexisting condition, since the plans they buy would have to cover them and follow the same consumer rules as other individual plans.

how_it_helps.text: The bill strikes the phrase excluding short-term limited-duration insurance from the ACA's definition of individual health insurance coverage, so those plans would be subject to the same requirements, including coverage of preexisting conditions [S2, S3].
The change would take effect for plan years beginning after December 31, 2018 [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Insurers selling short-term plans, who would lose their ability to sell cheaper, skimpier coverage exempt from ACA rules; buyers of those plans could face higher premiums in exchange for real coverage.

drawbacks.text: Bringing short-term plans under full ACA rules would raise their premiums, taking away the low-cost option that drew healthy people to them in the first place.
If short-term plans must follow all ACA rules, some may stop being offered at all, reducing choices for people who currently buy them.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core benefit is real: people buying these plans would be guaranteed coverage for preexisting conditions and full consumer protections instead of plans that can leave them with uncovered medical bills. The cost is that those plans would stop being cheap, and some might disappear. Whether that trade is worth it depends on how much weight you put on bare, cheap coverage versus coverage that actually pays when you get sick.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and sent to the Energy and Commerce Committee, which never held a hearing, reported it, or scheduled a vote before the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Raul Ruiz introduced the bill on July 24, 2018 [S1, S5].
It was referred to the House Committee on Energy and Commerce the same day, with no cosponsors [S4, S5].
No further action was taken before the 115th Congress ended on January 3, 2019, so the bill never reached the House floor [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Insurers selling short-term plans keep selling coverage exempt from ACA rules, without the preexisting-condition requirements the bill would have imposed.

for.role: Sponsor, House Energy and Commerce Committee member
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and referred it to committee; it received no cosponsors [S1, S4, S5].

sides.party_line_note: No vote was ever held and there were no cosponsors, so the partisan shape cannot be measured from the record.

industries.note: These insurers sell cheaper plans precisely by being exempt from ACA rules, including preexisting-condition protections; the bill would end that exemption. Their interest in the bill runs against consumers who need real coverage.

Competitors would no longer be able to skim healthy customers with exempt plans, and the rules would apply evenly. A level playing field also stabilizes the risk pool that keeps ACA-compliant premiums down.
